headline: Medium-risk shared-workspace and output-trust issues: AutoGen and Dify both write files and use broad egress, creating default interaction hazards.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and emits tool calls/code execution; Dify can ingest uploaded knowledge base files and tool outputs. If either agent consumes the other’s file-backed output as trusted instructions, prompt injection is plausible in default pairings. The shared-file pathway is documented in both profiles, so uncertainty does not justify a lower severity.
conditions: IF AutoGen writes instructions into a directory Dify later ingests as knowledge base content
IF Dify renders AutoGen-produced text as agent instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories
Disable automatic ingestion of newly written files
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files
Require manual review before Dify consumes AutoGen output
requires-engineering: enforce content-type and trust-boundary checks in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen touches application data and model-provider API keys, while Dify touches knowledge base content and conversation logs. Both have broad network egress and file access, so a shared workspace or copied artifacts can expose sensitive data across the pair. This is not provably blocked, and the default file-based interaction path is enough to keep it at medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or exported artifacts
IF AutoGen outputs secrets-bearing context into files Dify can ingest
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent
Redact secrets before file handoff
Restrict Dify uploads to approved file types
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on inter-agent transfers

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read and write files, and use broad network egress. AutoGen’s session scope is per-application process, while Dify shares state via server datastore; if both target the same mutable directory or resource, concurrent writes and race conditions can cause destructive conflicts. The overlap is substantial and dangerous by default when co-located.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git checkout
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking around shared mutable resources
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable concurrent edits to shared resources
Snapshot state before each agent run
requires-engineering: add resource-level locking in the orchestrator

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen produces tool calls and code-execution outputs that Dify can plausibly consume in workflows or agent steps. Dify’s agent/workflow tooling can then act on those outputs without an explicit verification layer. Because the pair is designed for agent chaining, the risk is a default trust cascade rather than a blocked pathway.
conditions: IF Dify uses AutoGen output as workflow input without validation
IF AutoGen-generated facts are forwarded into Dify tools or actions
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require citations for factual claims
Limit Dify actions to read-only tools
Log and review all cross-agent handoffs
requires-engineering: implement schema validation for agent outputs

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and application data, while Dify handles knowledge base content and conversation logs. The profiles do not specify residency or retention guarantees, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated data is routed through both systems. I cite both agents because the risk arises from their combined data handling, not one alone.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Dify knowledge bases or conversation logs
IF AutoGen or Dify is deployed under a residency or retention policy they do not satisfy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both systems
Review retention settings before deployment
Document data-flow boundaries
Purge logs after testing
requires-engineering: obtain vendor compliance attestations or DPA coverage
